Description: A collection of 102 inscribed pottery fragments, 63 of them legible, found by George Andrew Reisner's Harvard expedition in a storeroom beneath the royal acropolis of Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel. Written in ink in Paleo-Hebrew script, they are receipts for jars of aged wine and fine oil delivered to the palace, dated by regnal year and naming the clan districts they came from.
BiblicalSignificance: The ostraca name the clans of Manasseh — Abiezer, Shemida, Helek — the very families listed in Numbers 26 and settled in Joshua 17. A kingdom the Bible describes as wealthy and well-run left behind exactly the kind of palace bookkeeping you would expect: dated, measured, and filed by clan. They put ordinary Israelite names and harvests beside the royal story.
Interpretations: Scholars agree the ostraca are genuine eighth-century palace receipts; the clan names match Numbers 26, though the exact regnal years (ninth, tenth, fifteenth) are debated between kings.
